title: A Spectral Route to Directed-Polymer Glasses
authors: Sen Mu, Abbas Ali Saberi, Mehran Kardar
abstract: A finite density of mutually avoiding directed polymers in a quenched random medium is a minimal model of glassy line matter. The dilute theory, solved by replica Bethe ansatz, predicts an interaction free energy proportional to $ρ^2$ and disorder cumulants with distinct power-law dependences on the density $ρ$, but direct numerical tests have been hindered by the combinatorially large many-polymer transfer matrix. We recast the problem as filling logarithmic eigenvalues of a single-polymer transfer-matrix product, obtaining the quenched free energy, its cumulants, and a disorder-induced linear spectral edge consistent with the replica prediction.
summary: This paper develops a novel 'spectral route' to calculate the free energy of directed polymers in a random medium, modeling glassy line matter. By reformulating the problem as filling logarithmic eigenvalues of a transfer matrix product, the authors confirm that the resulting interaction energy scales quadratically with density ($ho^2$). This result successfully matches predictions from advanced theoretical methods like the replica Bethe ansatz.
main_problem: The study aims to determine the quenched free energy and its cumulants for a finite density of mutually avoiding directed polymers (DPRMs) in a random medium, which serves as a model for glassy line matter.
main_result: The spectral filling approach successfully reproduces the $ho^2$ interaction energy scaling predicted by the replica Bethe ansatz at low densities. Furthermore, it establishes that the disorder-induced linear edge of the logarithmic spectrum confirms this theoretical prediction.
method: The authors recast the complex many-polymer problem into an equivalent problem of filling the logarithmic eigenvalues of a single-polymer transfer matrix product, utilizing determinant identities and spectral analysis techniques.
model_or_system: The system models mutually avoiding directed polymers in a quenched random medium. This is mathematically formulated using a time-evolution governed by a single-polymer transfer matrix product $W(t) = T(t) \cdots T(1)$, whose minors relate to multi-polymer partition functions.
key_observables: Free-energy density ($f(ho)$), interaction free energy ($\Delta f(ho)$), and the disorder-averaged logarithmic spectral edge $\epsilon_0(t) - \epsilon_i(t)$.
important_parameters: Polymer density ($ho$), time $t$, and system size $N$. Key regimes include the dilute limit ($\Delta f(ho) \sim ho^2$) and the pure case ($\Delta f(ho) \sim ho^3$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the problem to a fermionic filling rule, requiring the transfer matrix product $W(t)$ to possess real positive eigenvalues, which is confirmed by combining total nonnegativity (from Boltzmann construction) and oscillatory matrix theory.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates DPRMs on a space-time lattice. Figure 2 shows the cumulative logarithmic growth rate vs. density $ho$, confirming linear scaling in the dilute regime. Figure 3 tracks the second disorder cumulant, showing expected low-density scaling and convergence at full filling.
paper_structure: The paper develops mathematically by first establishing the spectral connection using determinant identities (Chunk 3), then applying this to calculate the free energy density via eigenvalue filling (Chunks 1 & 2). Finally, it rigorously confirms the mathematical validity of the spectral method through high-precision numerical checks on the eigenvalues themselves (Chunk 4).
why_interesting: The connection between non-intersecting path counting (DPRMs) and random matrix theory spectra is highly relevant to understanding disordered quantum systems. The successful derivation of $ho^2$ scaling via spectral methods provides a powerful, alternative theoretical tool for analyzing glassy dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Finite-density mutually avoiding directed polymers in a quenched random medium. Colored paths connect or- dered endpoints at t = 0 and t = T on a space–time lattice with closed transverse boundary conditions, while the non- crossing constraint preserves their ordering. Red and blue spots indicate the quenched disorder. The lower-right block shows the bond-energy assignment defining T(s), with the two sides of each local cell carrying ±Es i and the neighboring cell carrying ±Es i−1.

FIG. 2. Mean cumulative growth per filled level, Fm(t)/(mt), as a function of the density ρ = m/N for N = 48 and 64 at the matched scaled times t/N 3/2 = 3/4 and 1. For N = 64, these correspond to t = 384 and 512, while for N = 48 the nearest integer times are t = 249 and 333. The close overlap of the curves at fixed t/N 3/2, as well as between the two scaled times, indicates an approximately stationary long-time regime. Inset: dilute-density regime ρ ≤1/4 at t/N 3/2 = 1. The dashed line is a linear fit to the N = 64 data, Fm(t)/(mt) = v1 −a1ρ, with v1 ≈4.2 and a1 ≈0.9; the N = 48 data closely follow the same relation. The numerical simulations use µ = 0 and σ = 2, with 14904 disorder...

FIG. 3. Second disorder cumulant of the filled free energy, F 2 m(t)c/(mt), as a function of the density ρ = m/N for N = 48 and 64 at the matched scaled times t/N 3/2 = 3/4 and 1. The sharp increase near full filling approaches the exact result F 2 N(t)c/(Lt) = 4σ2 = 16 for σ = 2. Inset: log-log plot of the dilute regime at t/N 3/2 = 1. The dashed line shows the fit a2ρ1/2 to the N = 64 data with a2 ≈2.9; the N = 48 data closely follow the same scaling.

FIG. 4. Rank-resolved logarithmic spectral edge. For this figure only, the levels are indexed as i = 0, . . . , N −1, with i = 0 denoting the largest logarithmic eigenvalue, and ϵi(t) = ln |λi(t)|/t. The main panel shows ϵ0(t) −ϵi(t) as a function of the scaled rank r = i/N for N = 48 and 64 at the matched scaled times t/N 3/2 = 3/4 and 1. Inset: log-log plot of the small-r regime 0 < r ≤1/4 at t/N 3/2 = 1. The dashed line is a linear fit to the N = 64 data, demonstrating ϵ0 −ϵi ∝r near the upper spectral edge; the N = 48 data closely follow the same scaling.
